chunks: Ali ibn Muhammad ibn Abdullah, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Khalid, from his father, from Fazalah ibn Ayyub, from the one who mentioned it, from Muhammad ibn Muslim, who said:

I was with Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) in the Mosque of the Messenger (peace be upon him and his family), so an overhang from the overhangs of the mosque fell and struck a man, but it did not harm him, and injured his leg. So Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) said: 'Ask him what he did today.' So they asked him, and he said: 'I went out, and in my sleeve was a date. So I passed by a beggar and gave him a date in charity.' So Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) said: 'By it, Allah repelled [the harm] from you.'

key_terms.شُرْفَةٌ: An overhang or projecting part of a building
key_terms.مَسْجِدُ الرَّسُولِ: The Mosque of the Messenger (Prophet Muhammad)

ai.seo_question: How does charity repel affliction according to Shia hadith?
ai.summary: In this narration from *Al-Kafi*, Imam al-Sadiq (peace be upon him) attributes the man's survival from a falling overhang in the Prophet's Mosque to his charity of a single date, illustrating the principle that *sadaqah* (charity) repels divine affliction (*bala'*). This incident highlights the Shia scholarly understanding that even minor acts of charity serve as a spiritual shield, transforming potential major calamities into minor, manageable injuries as an act of divine mercy.
